books.section: Topic 1.3 European exploration in the Americas
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: Both crowns believed the pope owned all newly discovered lands and could give them away at will
options.misconception: Overstates the pope's role; he claimed authority to divide lands between Catholic rulers, not ownership of them.

options.text: Both crowns still recognized the pope as an authority who could settle disputes between Catholic rulers
Both crowns had already broken with Rome and sought a neutral judge outside the Church
options.misconception: Puts the break with Rome too early; both crowns were Catholic in the 1490s.

options.text: Both crowns accepted the treaty only because the pope threatened excommunication against whichever side refused it
options.misconception: No threat of excommunication drove the treaty; both sides wanted a settlement and accepted the pope as judge.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what accepting a judge means. You only let someone settle your dispute if you recognize their authority to do it.
2. Ask what both crowns shared. Background from the books: both were Catholic, and both treated the pope as able to settle disputes between Catholic rulers.
3. Check the timing. The Reformation had not yet happened, so no break with Rome explains the treaty.
4. Rule out the overstatements. The pope assigned lands; he did not own them, and no threat forced the deal.
Remember: when rivals accept the same referee, ask what authority both sides still recognize.
rationales.B: Accepting the pope as judge only works if both sides see him as a real authority. The treaty shows papal authority still bound Catholic rulers in the 1490s.
rationales.A: The pope claimed the authority to assign lands between Catholic rulers; he did not own them. Ownership and the power to divide are not the same thing.
rationales.C: The break with Rome came with the Reformation, which began in 1517. In the 1490s both crowns were Catholic and the pope was their judge, not an outsider.
rationales.D: Both crowns wanted the dispute settled and chose the pope as mediator. The record shows acceptance, not a threat forcing the deal.

stem: The Treaty of Tordesillas was brokered with the pope's approval, and both Spain and Portugal accepted the division. What does their acceptance of papal mediation show about the Spanish and Portuguese crowns in the 1490s?

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494); the 370-league line west of the Cape Verde islands is the treaty's term.
stimulus.text: The 1494 agreement, brokered with the pope's approval, divided all newly discovered lands between the two Iberian crowns along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands.
